item.title: Public Enterprises portfolio shifted to Kamikamica from Charan Jeath Singh
item.description: Responsibility for Fiji’s public enterprises has been transferred from Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs, Culture, Heritage and Arts Charan Jeath Singh to newly sworn-in Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica as part of the latest Cabinet reshuffle. Kamikamica was sworn in yesterday as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce, Business Development and Public Enterprises, returni
item.content:encoded:
Responsibility for Fiji’s public enterprises has been transferred from Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs, Culture, Heritage and Arts Charan Jeath Singh to newly sworn-in Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica as part of the latest Cabinet reshuffle.

Kamikamica was sworn in yesterday as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce, Business Development and Public Enterprises, returning to Cabinet after previously serving in the portfolio.

The change means the Ministry of Public Enterprises is no longer under Charan Jeath Singh, who previously held the position of Minister for Public Enterprises, Multi-Ethnic Affairs, Culture, Heritage and Arts.

The Ministry of Public Enterprises is responsible for overseeing and implementing government reform programmes for state-owned enterprises while monitoring their performance and operations to improve efficiency and effectiveness. Its work is guided by the Public Enterprises Act 1996 and the Public Enterprises (Amendment) Act 2002.

The ministry oversees a significant portfolio of government commercial companies, including Fiji Broadcasting Corporation, Airports Fiji Limited, Fiji Public Trustee Corporation Limited, Food Processors (Fiji) Limited, Post Fiji Limited, Fiji Rice Limited, Unit Trust of Fiji Limited, Viti Corp Corporation Limited, Yaqara Pastoral Company Limited and Fiji Hardwood Corporation Limited.

It also has responsibility for several commercial statutory authorities, including the Fiji Electricity Authority, Fiji Meat Industry Board, Housing Authority, Maritime Safety Authority of Fiji, Water Authority of Fiji and the Public Rental Board.

In addition, the ministry oversees government’s majority-owned companies, including Fiji Pine Limited, Pacific Fishing Company Limited, Copra Millers Fiji Limited and Air Terminal Services.

The transfer of the portfolio restores responsibility for public enterprises to Kamikamica, who now assumes oversight of a range of key state-owned entities involved in aviation, utilities, agriculture, transport, housing and other strategic sectors of the economy.

item.title: Yasawa, Mamanuca declared fruit fly emergency areas
item.description: The Yasawa Group and Mamanuca Islands have been declared biosecurity emergency areas following the detection of the Tongan fruit fly ( Bactrocera facialis ), with strict controls now in place to prevent the pest’s spread. A notice published in the Fiji Gazette states that the declaration was made by the Minister for Agriculture and Waterways, Tomasi Tunabuna, under Section 77 of the Biosecurity Ac
item.content:encoded:
The Yasawa Group and Mamanuca Islands have been declared biosecurity emergency areas following the detection of the Tongan fruit fly ( Bactrocera facialis ), with strict controls now in place to prevent the pest’s spread.

A notice published in the Fiji Gazette states that the declaration was made by the Minister for Agriculture and Waterways, Tomasi Tunabuna, under Section 77 of the Biosecurity Act 2008, on the advice of the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF) and in consultation with the National Disaster Risk Management Council.

The declaration will remain in force for six months from the date of publication in the Gazette.

Under the emergency measures, the movement of a wide range of fruits, vegetables and host materials from the Yasawa Group and Mamanuca Islands is prohibited.

Restricted produce includes mangoes, guavas, papayas, citrus fruits, avocados, breadfruit, starfruit, roses, capsicum, tomatoes, pumpkins, zucchini, cucumbers, melons and other host materials identified by BAF.

The Gazette notice also states that host material includes all fruits found in the Yasawa Group and Mamanuca Islands.

The restrictions are aimed at containing the Tongan fruit fly and preventing it from spreading to other parts of Fiji, where it could pose a significant threat to agriculture and horticultural production.

The notice warns that any person who contravenes directions made under the declaration commits an offence under Sections 79(3) and 94 of the Biosecurity Act 2008 and is liable to the penalties prescribed under Schedule 5 of the Act.

The declaration was made on July 28, 2026, and is signed by Minister for Agriculture and Waterways Tomasi Tunabuna.

item.title: FNU Labasa campus to be renamed after Ratu Wiliame Katonivere
item.description: The Fiji National University’s Naiyaca Campus in Labasa will officially be renamed the Ratu Wiliame Katonivere Campus from today, in honour of the late Tui Macuata and former President of Fiji, Ratu Wiliame Katonivere. Ratu Wiliame will also officiate at the groundbreaking ceremony for the campus, marking another significant milestone in the university’s expansion in the Northern Division.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji National University’s Naiyaca Campus in Labasa will officially be renamed the Ratu Wiliame Katonivere Campus from today, in honour of the late Tui Macuata and former President of Fiji, Ratu Wiliame Katonivere.

Ratu Wiliame will also officiate at the groundbreaking ceremony for the campus, marking another significant milestone in the university’s expansion in the Northern Division.

The event will be the second groundbreaking ceremony held for the Labasa campus, highlighting FNU’s continued commitment to developing modern educational facilities in the North.

Located on Labasa’s main street in the Local Timber Building next to Courts Fiji Limited, the campus serves students from across Vanua Levu and nearby islands.

The campus currently offers programmes through three of the university’s colleges: the College of Humanities and Education, the College of Business, Hospitality and Tourism Studies, and the College of Engineering, Science and Technology.

The official renaming and groundbreaking ceremony are expected to bring together university officials, government representatives, traditional leaders, students and members of the public to celebrate the next phase of the campus’ development.

item.title: Calls for FCCC to handle banking consumer complaints
item.description: A former bank officer has called for stronger legal protections for banking customers by recommending that the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) be given authority to investigate and determine consumer complaints against licensed banks. In a submission to the parliamentary committee reviewing the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, Lautoka-based former bank office
item.content:encoded:
A former bank officer has called for stronger legal protections for banking customers by recommending that the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) be given authority to investigate and determine consumer complaints against licensed banks.

In a submission to the parliamentary committee reviewing the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, Lautoka-based former bank officer and trade unionist Sailesh Naidu said the legislation presented an opportunity to strengthen consumer protection by extending the FCCC’s jurisdiction to retail banking services.

Naidu argued that while the Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) should continue overseeing financial stability, licensing and prudential supervision of banks, complaints involving the treatment of individual banking customers should fall under the FCCC’s consumer protection mandate.

“Consumers require an independent body whose primary focus is protecting consumer rights,” Naidu said.

He said the FCCC was better placed to independently investigate complaints involving unfair treatment of consumers without creating any perception that the banking regulator’s primary concern was protecting the institutions it supervises.

“An independent complaint mechanism would strengthen public confidence in the financial system.”

Naidu said banking services were essential to almost every citizen and business in Fiji and customers should receive the same level of protection afforded to consumers in other industries.

“Banking customers should not have fewer consumer remedies simply because the service provider is a licensed financial institution,” he said.

He recommended that the Bill expressly recognise retail banking services as consumer services subject to FCCC oversight where consumer protection issues arise.

Under his proposal, the FCCC would have powers to investigate complaints relating to disputed fees and charges, require banks to provide relevant documents, make binding determinations where consumer protection laws have been breached, order refunds or compensation, and direct financial institutions to correct systemic practices that adversely affect consumers.

Naidu also said consumers needed a dispute resolution process that was affordable and accessible.

“Many banking disputes involve relatively small amounts of money. Consumers should not be forced to pursue lengthy or costly legal proceedings to recover fees or charges that have been incorrectly imposed.”

He proposed legislative amendments that would empower the FCCC to investigate complaints involving fees, misleading conduct, unfair practices and breaches of consumer protection laws, while requiring cooperation and information sharing between the FCCC and the Reserve Bank to avoid regulatory duplication.

Naidu said the proposed changes would strengthen confidence in Fiji’s banking system, improve accountability within financial institutions, provide consumers with an independent avenue for resolving disputes and reinforce the consumer protection objectives of the Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026.

He urged the parliamentary committee to consider amending the legislation accordingly, saying the changes would create “a stronger and more balanced consumer protection framework” while allowing the Reserve Bank to continue its core prudential and financial stability responsibilities.

item.title: ‘Fix it’
item.description: TUI Lau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara says the rescue of the six health workers and boat handler by authorities should not be labelled as a miracle and an issue to move on from. In a statement, Ratu Tevita called on Government to bring back dedicated health boats that used to service maritime islands decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
TUI Lau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara says the rescue of the six health workers and boat handler by authorities should not be labelled as a miracle and an issue to move on from.

In a statement, Ratu Tevita called on Government to bring back dedicated health boats that used to service maritime islands decades ago.

“The vanua o Lau gives thanks to God for the safe return of the six health workers and the boat handler of the MD Ono-i-Lau,” he said.

“And we thank the whole of Fiji, every community, who prayed for our people through those two nights, but we must not call this a miracle and move on.

“Those seven people were in the open sea for some thirty-six hours, holding onto the floorboards of their own boat, because a fibreglass hull with a 75-horsepower engine is what this country now provides for a medical outreach team crossing open ocean in our Lau waters.

“One man had to swim alone for hours towards Aiwa to find a mobile signal.”

He said that was not a rescue plan but a gamble with the lives of the people who keep our islands alive.

“It was not always so. In the 1970s and 1980s the government maintained designated health vessels for the maritime islands – the Nasi Yalo Dina, the Vuniwai ni Lau and others – proper boats, crewed and on a schedule, built for these waters and dedicated to the medical service.

“A nurse could reach her patients without risking her life to do it. Those vessels were withdrawn, and nothing of equal standing has replaced them.”

He said this was not the first time he had raised the issue with Government.

“On 26 June this year I wrote to the Prime Minister, to Ministers, to the Commissioner of Police and to the Commander of the RFMF, forwarding the Vanua Coast Watch concept and asking that it be resourced, beginning with a pilot in Lau.

“What we asked for was not a punt with an outboard on the back. It was proper observation craft, the first of them stationed at Lakeba, carrying marine VHF, satellite connectivity, tracking, drones and safety gear, and trained crews to work them.

“We proposed it against the drugs coming ashore, but a boat with a radio does not ask what the emergency is.”

Ratu Tevita called for Government to return the designated medical vessels, widen the subsidy for the Government Shipping Franchise Scheme and resource the Vanua Coast Watch and let the Lau pilot begin.

“Radios, trackers, drones, training and a few sound boats are what our communities are asking for. Set against the cost of one search across the Lau seascape, it is very little money.

“To those in Government, and to those who hope to be – do not carry this incident into the election campaign.

“Maritime Fiji has been knocking on closed doors over these boats for years, under more than one administration. I am asking that the door now be opened.

“Had a proper boat been under them, those seven would have come home on schedule. That is the standard we should be working to.”

item.title: Court clears former deputy prime minister
item.description: These were the words of acquitted former Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica after the Suva Magistrates Court yesterday ruled in favour of a no case to answer application. Speaking to the media, Mr Kamikamica said integrity had always been important to him and that the allegations made against him were inconsistent with his character.
item.content:encoded:
These were the words of acquitted former Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica after the Suva Magistrates Court yesterday ruled in favour of a no case to answer application.

Speaking to the media, Mr Kamikamica said integrity had always been important to him and that the allegations made against him were inconsistent with his character.

“Those who know me know that integrity is very important in my life,” he said, adding that government decisions he had been involved in were made with ethics and transparency.

Mr Kamikamica said his focus would now return to his public duties, including his role as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, and preparing for the upcoming election.

“There is a government to run, there are people to lead, and that’s where my focus will be.”

The former DPM also thanked his countless supporters and close family members for their support.

“I thank you all for all your support and all your prayers, and today we have restored truth and justice in this country.”

Magistrate Charles Ratakele upheld Mr Kamikamica’s no case to answer application, finding that FICAC had failed to adduce sufficient evidence on essential elements of both offences of perjury and giving false information to a public servant.

Addressing the perjury charge, Magistrate Ratakele found that the identity of Mr Kamikamica and the fact that he had been lawfully sworn during the Commission of Inquiry proceedings were not in dispute.

However, he found there was no evidence that Mr Kamikamica had made a material statement under oath.

He was charged with a count of perjury, alleging that he falsely stated under oath during the 2024 Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali that he had no knowledge of her appointment before it was publicly announced on September 5, 2024.

Mr Ratakele said the COI’s assisting counsel, Janet Mason, conceded during cross-examination that any prior knowledge of the appointment was outside the COI’s terms of reference and was not investigated.

He further noted Ms Mason accepted she never directly asked Mr Kamikamica whether he had prior knowledge of the appointment.

The magistrate said that, taken together with the evidence of the second prosecution witness, Government backbencher Kalaveti Ravu and the agreed facts, there was no evidence that the alleged statement was material to the COI proceedings.

On the element requiring proof that Mr Kamikamica knowingly made a false statement, Magistrate Ratakele found the prosecution relied heavily on diary entries belonging to Mr Ravu.

He ruled the diary entries had been admitted under a hearsay exception only to prove that the words had been written, not that the contents were true.

He also noted that Mr Ravu declined to explain or elaborate on the context of the conversations recorded in the diary.

Turning to the alternative charge of giving false information to a public servant, the magistrate again found there was no evidence capable of proving that the information allegedly given by Mr Kamikamica was false.

item.title: Union sounds alarm
item.description: A TOTAL of 360 teachers left the country for greener pastures between January 1 and May 31 in 2026. Fiji Teachers Union general secretary Muniappa Goundar said this meant an average of two teachers left every day within the five-month period.
item.content:encoded:
A TOTAL of 360 teachers left the country for greener pastures between January 1 and May 31 in 2026.

Fiji Teachers Union general secretary Muniappa Goundar said this meant an average of two teachers left every day within the five-month period.

“The total exit from the ministry from 1st January to 31st May is 360 which means an average of 72 teachers per month for the five first months of this year,” he said.

“If we break down further into days, the same five months have 154 days meaning an average of two teachers per day.”

He said this was concerning because the ministry was already struggling to retain teachers.

“We have to seriously look into this issue because our current population of teachers are being overwhelmed.”

Mr Goundar said while the ministry addressed this issue, they acknowledged Government’s efforts to look after current teachers.

He said the Government would soon pay teachers who took on acting roles and new graduate teachers.

“A total of approximately $1.698million will be paid out maybe in the 17th pay to 98 new appointments, 164 acting appointments and 12 nonteaching appointments.

“That means a total of 318 officers will be paid later this month.”

item.title: Book launch honours women parliamentarians’ legacy
item.description: THE history of Fiji’s Parliament cannot be fully told without recognising the contribution of women, says Speaker of Parliament Filimone Jitoko. Mr Jitoko acknowledged the contribution of women during the launch of the Celebrating Women in Parliament, 1966-2026, a booklet by the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians (CWP) Fiji Group in Suva yesterday.
item.content:encoded:
THE history of Fiji’s Parliament cannot be fully told without recognising the contribution of women, says Speaker of Parliament Filimone Jitoko.

Mr Jitoko acknowledged the contribution of women during the launch of the Celebrating Women in Parliament, 1966-2026, a booklet by the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians (CWP) Fiji Group in Suva yesterday.

He said the publication was more than a historical record, as it preserved the stories of women who broke barriers and helped shape Fiji’s democracy.

“It is part of our history and it should be kept for the future of our people to understand how democracy grew out of this country and especially the contribution of women to the growth of democracy,” he said.

The Speaker of the House highlighted the contribution of Fiji’s first women parliamentarians, Adi Losalini Raravuya, Loloma Livingston and Irene Jai Narayan, who entered Parliament in 1966.

“It is not a matter of just trying to fill the numbers, but it is the contribution of women themselves in the process of being part of the decision-making process.”

CWP Fiji Group deputy chairperson Premila Kumar said the publication was created to preserve stories that could have been lost over time.

Ms Kumar said compiling the booklet was challenging as information about former women parliamentarians was scattered across different sources.

“People had memories, but once you go, the memories go too,” she said.

Mr Jitoko said the publication should inspire future generations of women and girls to consider leadership and public service.

“I hope that every young woman and girl who reads this publication will see more than photographs and biographies. I hope they will see possibilities.”
